text: You're given a tree of n nodes as an edge list. If you root the tree at a node, it has some height. Return all the nodes that, when chosen as root, give the minimum possible height.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the answer is the tree's center, and a tree's center is always one or two nodes. So I'm returning at most two roots. Is that right?
Correct — one or two. It's guaranteed to be a valid tree.

Let me run through an example. A path zero, one, two, three, four, five. Rooting at an end like zero gives height five; rooting near the middle is shorter. The two middle nodes, two and three, both give the minimum, so the answer is two and three. With an odd number of nodes there'd be a single center.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. The brute force is to root at every node and BFS its height — n squared. This problem reminds me of topological sort, run in reverse on an undirected tree: the center is the midpoint of the tree's longest path, and I can find it by peeling leaves inward. Repeatedly remove all current leaves, degree one, one whole layer at a time, until at most two nodes remain — those are the centers. That's linear time.

Here's the plan. One: handle n of one and two up front, then build the adjacency list and degrees, and queue every leaf. Two: while more than two nodes remain, peel one whole layer, and push any neighbor whose degree drops to one. Three: return whatever is left in the queue. One thing worth flagging — the loop condition is remaining n greater than two, not queue non-empty. The centers' degrees also drop to one and they enter the queue, so if I peeled until empty I'd delete the centers too. Tracking the remaining count and stopping at two or fewer is what keeps them. And the queue size snapshot binds one layer together, so I don't mix the next layer into the current peel. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. Two early returns, then adjacency plus degree, and every degree-one node goes in the queue. Each round I snapshot the layer size, subtract it from n, pop that many leaves, and decrement each neighbor's degree. When the loop stops, the queue holds the answer. That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — a neighbor joins the queue the moment its degree hits one, not zero: degree one means it just became a leaf and is next to peel.

Let's dry-run on the path zero to five, expecting two and three. I start with leaves zero and five, and n equals six. Each layer strips both ends, so n goes six, four, two. The row that matters is the stop: n is two, the loop exits, and the queue holds two and three — exactly the centers, because the leaves peel symmetrically from both ends and converge. Corner cases: n of one gives zero, and n of two gives zero and one, handled up front, since with fewer than three nodes there's nothing to peel.

Time is linear — a tree has n minus one edges and each node is peeled once. Space is linear for the adjacency list, degree array, and queue. Oh, one more thing — if I also wanted the actual minimum height, I'd count the peel layers: that's the height when one center is left, plus one when two are left. And this leaf-peeling is the undirected-tree cousin of Kahn's topological sort, which peels in-degree-zero nodes in a directed graph.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You recognized the answer as the tree center — one or two nodes. You peeled leaves layer by layer and stopped on the remaining count, not an empty queue, so the centers survive. And you bound each layer with a size snapshot. Good work.
